subject: internet-packets
title: Packets, Protocols, and a Network of Networks
summary: Why the internet chops data into packets and lets each network be different.

keys.prompt: What was Bob Kahn's "open architecture" idea?
keys.answer: Link independent networks of any design with one shared protocol that carries packets between them.

keys.prompt: Why was the original TCP split into TCP and IP?
keys.answer: Some apps, like voice, would rather skip a lost packet than wait. So IP handles addressing and forwarding, and TCP adds extras like recovery.

keys.prompt: How is packet switching different from an old phone call?
keys.answer: A call holds one line open the whole time; packets share the network, each traveling on its own.

cards.title: Built to connect anything
cards.text: The internet was designed to connect networks that worked in totally different ways, including radio and satellite networks. How do you build one system on top of all of them?

cards.question: The internet had to connect networks that worked in totally different ways. How do you think that was done?

options.text: Make every network use the same hardware
Let each network stay different and share one protocol
Replace them all with one giant network

cards.reveal: Bob Kahn's 1972 "open architecture": each network stays different, and one shared protocol carries packets between them. He and Vint Cerf began designing it in 1973.

cards.title: Packet switching
cards.text: Instead of holding one line open for a whole conversation, like an old phone call, data is cut into packets that share the network. Leonard Kleinrock published the first paper on packet-switching theory in 1961 and argued that packets could work in place of reserved circuits.
cards.example: ARPANET's first node went live at UCLA in September 1969. By the end of that year, four host computers were connected.

cards.title: Open architecture
cards.text: In 1972, Bob Kahn proposed linking many independent networks of any design. Each network could stay different. A shared protocol would carry packets between them. In 1973, he and Vint Cerf began designing that protocol, TCP.

cards.title: TCP and IP split up
cards.text: The original TCP did everything. Then real uses, like sending voice in the 1970s, showed some apps would rather skip a lost packet than wait. So it split in two: IP handles addresses and forwarding, and TCP handles extras like recovering lost packets and controlling flow.
cards.example: Delivery is "best effort." If a packet does not arrive, the sender sends it again.

why.q: Why split IP from TCP instead of one protocol doing everything?
why.a: Apps want different things: live voice would rather skip a lost packet, while a file needs every piece. A simple IP lets each app choose.

cards.title: Switch day
cards.text: On January 1, 1983, the ARPANET switched its hosts to TCP/IP. Electronic mail turned out to be one of the biggest impacts of that era. By 1992, the internet had one million hosts.

cards.question: The internet's designers kept the core simple and let the "smarts" live in the computers at each end. What are the trade-offs of that design, for innovation and for security?
nudges: Who gets to build new apps if the network does not need to approve them?
What problems does a simple, open core make harder?

questions.q: Why was IP split from TCP?

options.text: Some apps, like voice, would rather handle lost packets themselves than wait.
options.why: Right. IP became the simple addressing and forwarding layer.

options.text: TCP was too slow to send email.
options.why: The issue was about apps like packet voice, not email.
The split was about flexibility, not privacy.

questions.q: What was Bob Kahn's "open architecture" idea?

options.text: Link independent networks of any design with a shared protocol
Make every network use the same hardware
options.why: The opposite: networks could be different.

options.text: Let anyone open the ARPANET's computers
options.why: It was about connecting networks, not opening machines.

options.text: The network tries, and lost packets are resent by the source.
options.why: Right. Reliability comes from the ends, not a promise from the network.

options.text: Every packet is guaranteed to arrive on time.
options.why: No guarantee. That is why retransmission exists.
All packets are sent. Some may be lost and resent.
